To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the apparent age of North Atlantic surface water was larger than that of today by 820 ±430 to 1 010 ±340 years at the beginning of the Holocene, and that the apparent age was larger by 1 230 ± 600 years at the end point of the Heinrich stadial 1 event.

the apparent age of North Atlantic surface waters has varied by more than 1,000 years over the last 20,000 year, and that the reservoir age of the North Atlantic is largest at the end of Heinrich stadials and during the Younger Dryass, and is lowest during the Bølling and Allerød periods.

the apparent age of the surface water in the North Atlantic Ocean has varied significantly in the past, and that these variations have important implications for the interpretation of radiocarbon dates in this region.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing of the last glaciation and the mechanisms governing it.
the timing of the deglaciation in the North Atlantic.
the reconstruction of the timing of the last glacial–interglacial transition and the associated climate changes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the deglacial chronologies from Greenland ice cores and North Atlantic marine records are now in agreement.
there is no evidence for a change in the reservoir age in the Atlantic during the last deglaciations, and that the reservoir age was constant at least in the Atlantic north of 30° N.
the deglaciation started around 19.5 ka, and that the Bølling/Allerød was the warmest period during the deglaciation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there was a large reservoir effect in the North Atlantic at the end of Heinrich events and at the end of cold periods, but not in between.

the apparent age of North Atlantic surface water was large (1,200 years) at the end of Heinrich 1 (15,000 BP), and that the reservoir effect was small (less than 200 years) during the warm period between Heinrich 1 and Younger Dryas.

the apparent age of the surface ocean in the northern North Atlantic was significantly higher than today during the end of Heinrich 1 and during the Younger Dry as, but was close to today’s during the warm Bøling–Allerød interstadial period.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reservoir ages are highly variable and need to be corrected in marine records from the North Atlantic.
the timing of the last glacial termination is not as straightforward as it might seem.
we can now use the same calendar age scale for the marine and terrestrial records of the last deglication.
